description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de la Universidad Americana interesados en vivir una experiencia real de trabajo en equipo con el fin de utilizar nuestras habilidades para resolver un reto en especifico.
summary: TerraShift is a decision-support web tool for smallholder farmers in Nicaragua's Dry Corridor. It compares three management strategies for maize and beans (E1 traditional, E2 water conservation and E3 soil regeneration) under normal years, dry years and a prolonged mid-summer dry spell (canicula). Everything is computed directly from NASA data: daily rainfall and temperature from NASA POWER feed a simple FAO-56 and FAO-33 water-balance model, while SMAP soil moisture and MODIS and Landsat vegetation indices show how the zone has actually behaved. An automated pipeline updates the data daily and a public API serves it. The web page shows a three-line summary and a plain-language explanation built from fixed, transparent rules, with NASA trends and a short-term projection; no AI model runs in the product. Visitors can also draw and propose new study zones on a map. TerraShift helps farmers and technicians see how much a drought could cost each practice and which one holds up best, using open data. Results are estimates with uncertainty, not field measurements.
details:
What it does. TerraShift lets a farmer or technician pick a study zone in Nicaragua's Dry Corridor and compare three strategies for maize and beans: E1 traditional, E2 water conservation and E3 soil regeneration. For each crop and each type of year (normal, dry, prolonged dry spell) it shows the relative yield, water stress, transpiration deficit and effective rainfall, with the range observed across years. A three-line summary and a plain-language explanation say which practice holds up best and how confident the result is.

How it works. A Python pipeline downloads NASA POWER daily weather and, through the AppEEARS service, SMAP soil moisture and MODIS and Landsat (HLS) vegetation indices, and stores them in PostgreSQL with PostGIS. A water-balance model (Hargreaves-Samani evapotranspiration, FAO-56 crop coefficients, a soil water bucket and the FAO-33 yield response) is run on the observed years of the zone. The three strategies share the same weather and differ only in runoff, soil evaporation and water-holding capacity. A Java 21 Spring Boot API serves the results and a static web page, published on GitHub Pages, displays them with charts and an interactive Leaflet map.

The explanation. The text shown to farmers comes from a JSON file of about 120 conditional rules and more than 30 recommendations. The rules use the results, NASA trends (recent years against earlier ones), a linear projection of annual rainfall and a risk score, and every sentence shows the criterion that triggered it. No AI model runs inside the product.

Benefits and impact. It turns open NASA data into a concrete question a farmer can ask: how much would a dry year cost me with each practice? It works for any zone drawn on the map once the team approves it, and the data update by themselves every day.

Creativity. The three strategies are compared under the same observed climate, so the difference comes only from management. Transparent rules replace a black box, and each recommendation can be traced to the data that triggered it.

What we considered. Soil parameters and the effect of each practice are model assumptions, not field measurements, and the page says so. Results are estimates with uncertainty and do not replace an agronomist.

Tools. Python 3.10+, PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS, Java 21 and Spring Boot, JavaScript, Leaflet, Docker, GitHub Pages and systemd timers for the daily sync.
dataRefs: SMAP L4 Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP v008)
MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 and Landsat HLS HLSL30 v020, via AppEEARS
projectRefs: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998)
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33 (Doorenbos and Kassam, 1979)
